node.label: Winona Wheeler
node.date_label: 'The Othering of Indigenous History' 1998 · 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' 2005 · 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' 2010 · Shekon Neechie 2018 · open letter 2021
node.description: Historian of Cree oral tradition and of the academy's treatment of Indigenous history. In 1998 she argued that historians of 'Indian–White relations', relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist frame. Her method writing treats Indigenous oral history 'as source and method in scholarly research': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', and the historian 'develops reciprocal relationships with them'. Oral historians, she argues, must learn how knowledge keepers establish their sources ('a traditional footnote'), and the historian's task is 'to apply the teachings that guide the learning, keeping, and transmission of Indigenous knowledge' (2010). She learned from Stan Cuthand, Ahenakew's protégé, and draws on Ahenakew's published account of Old Men as historians. Leddy (2010) opens her account of community-based history with Wheeler's words on knowledge 'by way of relationships'. She serves on the managing board of Shekon Neechie (2018).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Winona Wheeler (b. 1958; published as Winona Stevenson in the 1990s); 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History' (Saskatchewan History, 1998); 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' (in Walking a Tightrope, 2005); 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' (in The West and Beyond, 2010). University of Saskatchewan (Native/Indigenous Studies) from 1988; First Nations University of Canada from 1996.
node.scope_note: Read in full: 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' (AU Press, open access, 2010); the 1998 Saskatchewan History essay (earlier reading); Leddy 2010; the 2018 USask news story; the 2021 open letter. Unread: the 2005 'Reflections' chapter (known through her own n. 1 and Leddy), Part III of 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories' (1999), her Berkeley dissertation (2000) and later co-authored work. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: cited by 8 Canadian History PhDs as Wheeler and 17 as Stevenson (the name keys are not merged); context only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Indigenous oral history 'as source and method': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', relations are reciprocal, and historians must 'apply the teachings'.
proposed_edges.map_label: Oral history as source and method
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 47 ('Elders are not just repositories of knowledge. They are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers'), p. 48 ('The overarching goal of this paper is to contribute to the growing studies on the value of Indigenous oral history as source and method in scholarly research'; 'one develops reciprocal relationships with them'), p. 59 ('our task is not only to create a space for other ways of knowing as an object or subject of study, but also to create a space to apply the teachings').

proposed_edges.relationship: Wheeler takes Ahenakew's account of the Old Man as historian and 'authentic repository for the annals of his people', and learned from his protégé Stan Cuthand.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 49 (Cuthand 'followed the path of his mentor Edward Ahenakew'; she met Cuthand in 1982 at Manitoba), p. 53 (Ahenakew, The Plains Cree, on the Old Man as 'an institution in Indian life through the centuries') and p. 56 ('an authentic repository for the annals of his people').

proposed_edges.relationship: Historians of 'Indian–White relations', relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist frame and set Indigenous oral history aside (1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler] 1998, pp. 24–27, read in full (existing nnreq_stevenson_1998, on the native_newcomer roster). Person-level edge beside edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer), which stays. Ends in Agent A's field; A to confirm.

proposed_edges.relationship: Knowledge keepers establish source and transmission within their narratives, 'sort of like a "traditional footnote"': oral history needs its own source criticism, learned from the keepers themselves.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 58: 'Cree historians trained in the oral tradition do not assume omniscient authority'; side stories 'serve to establish the original source(s)' — 'It's sort of like a "traditional footnote."' The narratives and protocols she discusses are not reproduced (OCAP review #1).

proposed_edges.relationship: Cree intellectual traditions written 'in history, as history'; co-founder of the Indigenous-controlled Shekon Neechie.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 48 ('as we carve a space for Indigenous oral history in history, as history'); USask News 2018 on the managing board. Ends in Agent B's field; B to confirm.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Leddy has no entry; the influence is recorded in the serpent_river_collaboration strand and Leddy's roster row.

Her statements of method are used (oral history 'as source and method', p. 48; elders 'are not official documents', p. 47; reciprocal relationships, p. 48; the 'traditional footnote', p. 58; to 'apply the teachings', p. 59; Stan Cuthand and Ahenakew, pp. 49, 53, 56). The narratives, protocols, teachings and family material the chapter publishes are not used (OCAP review #1). n. 1 cites her 2005 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' (unread).
